observations: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
B1: Preview banner: “Evaluation preview · learning history and analytics are not saved.”
B2: Prediction: two already-sorted piles of four cards, “what is the most comparisons you could ever need?”; choices7/16/28; selected16 and locked.

B3: Exploration: “Which top card is smaller?” with Take10from pileA and Take4from pileB; opened “Where did the piles come from?”; rounds show singles0comparisons, pairs4, sorted piles6; “The last merge adds at most7.”

B4: Deliberately clicked Take10 instead of4: “The other top card is smaller, so it goes first. Each card placed while both piles have cards is one comparison.”; no placement or counter change observed.

B5: Took4 then5 fromB then10 fromA; merged row4 5 10; COMPARISONS3 PLACED3/8; clicked Finish for me; intermediate5/8 and comparisons5, then final sorted4 5 10 18 20 21 23 36; “Merged with7comparisons.”; whole sort0+4+6+7=17 against28.
B6: Desktop screenshot after rounds opened showed top rounds clipped inside scrolling stage while active piles/counters and bottom instruction remained visible.

B7: Reveal: “Not quite: it was ‘7’.”; each comparison looks at two top cards and places smaller permanently; at most7 for8cards; “once a pile empties, the rest slides over free”; interleaving needs all7; whole sort17 vs28; 1,000cards under10,000comparisons vs499,500.

prediction.reason: The maximum-comparison question offers plausible competing counts and makes the already-sorted prerequisite explicit.

interaction.reason: Choosing smaller top cards visibly advances a sorted row and counter, with specific correction for an incorrect choice.

payoff.reason: The reveal connects the seven counted placements to the empty-pile bound and the whole-sort saving.

clarity.reason: Core actions are clear, but the additional rounds produce clipped content and the maximum answer appears before the merge is performed.

transfer.reason: The reveal extends the same merging principle to1,000cards with explicit comparison costs, an editorial application rather than observed learning.

accessibility.reason: No keyboard, phone, contrast, zoom/reflow or reduced-motion checks were performed.
evidence: Desktop AX snapshots and screenshots only; accessible labels observed but insufficient for an accessibility rating.

surprise.reason: The committed16 guess is contradicted by a seven-comparison visible merge and supported bound.

visualExplanation.reason: Moving values from two piles into a growing ordered row centrally exposes the merge operation.

playfulness.reason: The learner can test a wrong top card and choose cards, but the successful sequence is tightly constrained.

practicalValue.reason: The experience gives disciplinary value in reasoning about sorting cost rather than an everyday action.

depth.reason: It connects local comparisons, empty-pile completion, prior rounds and larger-input costs.

complexity.reason: Against the declared boundary, the learner must distinguish maximum versus observed counts, sorted-input invariants, pairwise baselines and multiple sorting rounds.
complexity.boundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no map-projection, sorting-algorithm or sound-propagation theory assumed.

whyCool: Taking the smaller top cards builds a full sorted row with seven comparisons while the whole-sort ledger totals17against28.
caveat: Only one generated pile pair was observed; the early-exhaustion boundary is explained in text and the final five cards were auto-completed.
